entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of England — founded in 1534 when King Henry VIII broke with Rome following the Pope's refusal to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon — is both the mother church of the worldwide Anglican Communion (approximately 85 million members across 165 countries) and the established church of England, with the British monarch as its Supreme Governor and the Archbishop of Canterbury as its spiritual leader, making it one of the most institutionally significant Christian churches in the world.

The Church of England's founding in the English Reformation created a distinctively English form of Christianity that attempted to occupy a middle way ('via media') between Roman Catholicism and continental Protestantism: retaining the episcopal structure (bishops), liturgy (the Book of Common Prayer, 1549, one of the most influential texts in the English language), and sacramental theology of Catholicism, while rejecting papal authority and incorporating Protestant theological emphases on scripture and faith. The Elizabethan Settlement (1559) defined this compromise in ways that have largely persisted.

The Church of England's modern challenges are profound: declining attendance (from approximately 40% weekly attendance in the 1960s to approximately 2-3% in recent years), debates about women's ordination (women ordained as priests since 1994, as bishops since 2014), same-sex relationships, and decolonization of its liturgy and governance. Its global Anglican Communion is deeply divided between conservative African provinces (opposing same-sex blessings) and progressive Western provinces, with the 2022 Lambeth Conference revealing possibly irreconcilable divisions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of England — founding the Anglican Communion through Henry VIII's break with Rome, creating the Book of Common Prayer that shaped the English language — is one of history's most consequential religious institutions whose establishment triggered the English Reformation and shaped modern English-speaking culture.
